cards.back: Above, excessive (hypertension)
Below, deficient (hypoglycemia)
Brady- = slow; tachy- = fast (bradycardia, tachypnea)
Without, absence of (apnea, anemia)
Difficult, painful, abnormal (dyspnea, dysuria)
Poly- = many, much (polyuria); oligo- = few, scanty (oliguria)
Hemi- = half (hemiplegia); peri- = around (pericardium)
Endo- = within; epi- = upon/above; sub- = below/under (subcutaneous)
Inter- = between; intra- = within (intravenous)
Inflammation (appendicitis)
-ectomy = surgical removal; -otomy = cutting into; -ostomy = creating an opening
Blood condition (hypoxemia, anemia)
Pain (neuralgia)
Breathing (apnea, dyspnea, tachypnea)
-megaly = enlargement (cardiomegaly); -oma = tumor/mass
-osis = abnormal condition (cyanosis); -penia = deficiency (leukopenia)
-rrhage = bursting forth/bleeding (hemorrhage); -rrhea = flow/discharge (diarrhea)
Heart, lung, liver
Kidney, stomach, head
Blue, blood, skin
Anterior (ventral) = front of body; posterior (dorsal) = back
Superior = toward the head (above); inferior = toward the feet (below)
Medial = toward the midline; lateral = away from the midline, toward the side
Proximal = closer to the trunk/point of attachment; distal = farther from it
Ipsilateral = same side of the body; contralateral = opposite side
Palmar = palm of the hand; plantar = sole of the foot
Vertical plane dividing body into right and left; midsagittal splits it into equal halves
Vertical plane dividing body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) parts
Horizontal plane dividing body into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) parts
Supine = lying face up on back; prone = lying face down
Sitting up, about 45-60 degrees (high Fowler's more upright); semi-Fowler's about 30-45
Supine on an incline with head lower than feet; modified = flat with legs raised. Rarely used for shock now; follow local protocol
Lateral recumbent (on side) to protect the airway of an unresponsive, breathing patient without spinal injury

cards.front: Blood flow through the heart: right side
cards.back: Vena cavae > right atrium > tricuspid valve > right ventricle > pulmonic valve > pulmonary artery > lungs
Lungs > pulmonary veins > left atrium > mitral (bicuspid) valve > left ventricle > aortic valve > aorta > body
Arteries carry blood away from the heart (usually oxygenated); veins return blood to the heart. Exception: pulmonary vessels
Delivery of oxygen and nutrients to cells and removal of waste products; inadequate perfusion = shock
Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume
Red cells (carry O2), white cells (immunity), platelets (clotting), plasma (liquid portion)
Epidermis (outer), dermis (middle: nerves, vessels, glands), subcutaneous tissue (fat, deepest)
Nose/mouth > pharynx > larynx (epiglottis, vocal cords) > trachea
Trachea > mainstem bronchi > bronchioles > alveoli (site of gas exchange)
Diaphragm contracts and flattens, ribs lift; chest volume rises, pressure falls, air flows in (active); exhalation is passive

cards.front: Oxygen in room air vs exhaled air
cards.back: Room air about 21% O2; exhaled air about 16% O2 (enough for rescue breathing)
Oxygen and CO2 diffuse across the alveolar-capillary membrane by concentration gradient
Aerobic uses oxygen and yields much energy; anaerobic (no oxygen) yields little energy and produces lactic acid
7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral (fused), 4 coccyx (fused) = 33 vertebrae
Skeletal (voluntary), smooth (involuntary, in organs/vessels), cardiac (involuntary, heart only)
CNS = brain and spinal cord; PNS = nerves outside CNS (sensory and motor)
Sympathetic = fight or flight (raises HR, BP); parasympathetic = rest and digest (lowers HR)
Liver, gallbladder (also part of colon)
Stomach, spleen (also pancreas tail)
Appendix, cecum (right ovary/fallopian tube in females)
Kidneys, pancreas, aorta, vena cava; behind the peritoneal lining
Insulin, made by beta cells of the pancreas; glucagon raises glucose
Carotid, femoral, radial, brachial (infants), posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis
SA node in the right atrium is the natural pacemaker (60-100 bpm)
Systole = ventricular contraction (top BP number); diastole = ventricular relaxation/filling (bottom number)
Eye opening (1-4), verbal (1-5), motor (1-6); total 3-15, lower = worse
In some chronic lung disease patients, low O2 is the breathing stimulus; never withhold O2 from a hypoxic patient
Adequate: 12-20, regular, clear lungs, good chest rise. Inadequate: rate extremes, shallow, retractions, cyanosis, noisy
Meninges: dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater; cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain
Scene size-up, primary assessment, history taking, secondary assessment, reassessment
Scene safety, PPE/BSI, mechanism of injury/nature of illness, number of patients, additional resources, spinal consideration
General impression, level of consciousness, airway, breathing, circulation (bleeding, pulse, skin), priority/transport decision

cards.front: Life threats addressed first in primary
cards.back: Life-threatening bleeding, airway, breathing and circulation problems; treat as found
Alert, responds to Verbal stimuli, responds to Painful stimuli, Unresponsive
Signs/symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Pertinent past history, Last oral intake, Events leading up
Onset, Provocation/Palliation, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity (0-10), Time
Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures/Penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, Swelling
A relevant sign/symptom the patient does not have (e.g., denies chest pain in dyspnea patient); document it
Every 5 minutes (or more often)
Every 15 minutes
Repeat primary assessment, reassess vitals, recheck interventions, reconfirm transport priority, recheck chief complaint
Ejection, death in same vehicle, intrusion >12 in at occupant site, fall >10 ft (all ages, ACS 2021), pedestrian/cyclist thrown or run over, motorcycle crash with significant impact
Quick head-to-toe exam for significant MOI/unresponsive trauma patient, looking for DCAP-BTLS
Facial droop, arm drift, abnormal speech; any one abnormal suggests stroke
Signs of increased work of breathing; tripod positioning and nasal flaring also indicate respiratory distress
High-pitched whistling, often expiratory; seen with asthma/COPD (lower airway narrowing)
High-pitched sound on inspiration; upper airway obstruction (croup, foreign body, swelling)
Bubbling/crackling lung sounds suggesting fluid in alveoli (pulmonary edema, pneumonia)
Low-pitched, rattling sounds from secretions in larger airways
Flail segment moves opposite to the rest of the chest (in on inhalation, out on exhalation); 2+ adjacent ribs each broken in 2+ places
Hypertension (widening pulse pressure), bradycardia, irregular respirations; sign of raised intracranial pressure
Bruising behind the ear / around the eyes; signs of basilar skull fracture
Late signs of tension pneumothorax or other obstructive problems
Crepitus under skin from air in tissue; suggests airway/chest injury
Primary, history (SAMPLE, OPQRST), secondary focused on complaint, vitals, interventions, transport, reassess
Primary, rapid head-to-toe exam, vitals, SAMPLE from family/bystanders/records, then interventions and transport
Reason EMS was called, in the patient's own words
Gives conditions/medications/allergies when the patient cannot give history
60-100 beats/min
12-20 breaths/min
Systolic about 90-140, diastolic about 60-90 (ranges vary by source); hypotension is usually systolic <90
About 94-100% on room air (many texts: 95-100%). Below 94%: give O2 and titrate to 94-99% per protocol (COPD targets often 88-92%)
Systolic minus diastolic; narrows in shock, widens with rising intracranial pressure
About 98.6 F (37 C); roughly 97.8-99.1 F
About 70-120 mg/dL (ranges vary by source). Hypoglycemia treatment threshold is commonly <60-70 mg/dL with symptoms; per local protocol
HR about 100-160; RR about 25-50 (newborns 30-60); SBP about 70-100. Ranges vary by textbook; learn your course's table
HR about 90-150; RR about 20-30 (some tables 24-40); SBP about 80-100. Ranges vary by source
HR about 80-140; RR about 20-30 (some tables 22-34); SBP about 80-110. Ranges vary by source
HR about 70-120; RR about 15-25 (some tables 18-30); SBP about 80-120. Ranges vary by source
HR about 60-100; RR about 12-20; SBP about 90-130 (near adult values). Ranges vary by source
70 + (2 x age in years) for ages 1-10; below this = hypotension. Infants under 1 yr: <70; over 10 yr: <90. A falling BP is a late sign in children
Blue-gray skin or mucosa from poor oxygenation
Pale skin from poor perfusion/blood loss
Yellow skin/sclera; liver problems
Fever, heat exposure, allergic reaction, CO poisoning (cherry red; rare)
Blotchy discoloration; poor perfusion/late shock
Warm, dry, pink (check mucosa/nail beds in dark skin); normal capillary refill is 2 seconds or less
Most reliable in infants and children under 6; unreliable in cold or elderly adults
Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light
Opioids (narcotics); also organophosphate/nerve agent poisoning and some brainstem strokes
Fear, drugs (stimulants), hypoxia, cardiac arrest, certain brain injury
Possible head injury/stroke (also may be normal variation or prosthesis)
Rate, rhythm (regular/irregular), quality (strong/weak/thready/bounding)
Rate, rhythm, quality (breath sounds, chest expansion), effort
Unreliable with CO poisoning, cold extremities, shock, nail polish, motion; treat patient, not the number
Count breaths for 30 seconds and multiply by 2 (or 60 seconds if irregular); do it without telling patient
Systolic only; used when auscultation is not possible
Tachycardia >100/min; bradycardia <60/min
Right patient, medication, dose, route, time, documentation (many programs add right reason)
Generic = official nonproprietary name (e.g., albuterol), not capitalized; trade = manufacturer's brand name (e.g., Proventil)
Indication = reason to give; contraindication = reason NOT to give
Tablet, capsule, solution, suspension (shake first), gel, inhaler, powder, gas, sublingual, injectable
Enteral = through the GI tract (oral); parenteral = outside the GI tract (injection)

cards.front: Medication routes: EMT vs beyond EMT scope
cards.back: EMT: oral, sublingual, inhaled, intranasal, IM (auto-injector), per protocol. Know but beyond EMT scope in most states: IV, IO, subcutaneous, rectal
Hypoxia (SpO2 <94%), respiratory distress, shock; titrate to 94-99%. NRB 10-15 L/min; nasal cannula 1-6 L/min. Chest pain alone with normal SpO2 does not require O2
None for a hypoxic or critically ill patient; avoid unnecessary high-flow if SpO2 normal (per protocol)
Conscious patient with altered mental status and known/suspected hypoglycemia who can swallow
Unresponsive or unable to swallow/protect airway; one tube (about 15 g, varies by product) buccal/oral, repeat per protocol
Chest pain suggestive of heart attack (ACS)
162-324 mg chewed (2-4 low-dose 81 mg tablets; commonly 324 mg), non-enteric-coated, per protocol
Aspirin/NSAID allergy, active GI bleeding or ulcer, unable to swallow; not for children; per protocol, other bleeding disorders
Chest pain of suspected cardiac origin in a patient with their own prescribed NTG; vasodilator that reduces heart workload
0.4 mg sublingual (tablet or spray); may repeat every 5 min to a max of 3 doses (including doses the patient took) if BP stays adequate; per medical direction
SBP below 90-100 (cutoff per local protocol); PDE5 inhibitor use: sildenafil/vardenafil within 24 h, tadalafil within 48 h; head injury; already took max dose
Headache, hypotension, dizziness, burning under tongue
Anaphylaxis / severe allergic reaction (respiratory distress or shock signs)
Adult 0.3 mg (about 30 kg and up); pediatric 0.15 mg (about 15-30 kg); infant 0.1 mg device where available; IM into anterolateral thigh; repeat per protocol
Tachycardia, anxiety, pallor, tremor, hypertension, palpitations
Wheezing/bronchospasm in asthma or COPD (bronchodilator)
90 mcg per puff, usually 1-2 puffs, per protocol (patient-prescribed MDI)
Tachycardia, tremor, nervousness
Suspected opioid overdose with respiratory depression/altered mentation
Intranasal: 4 mg spray in one nostril, or 2 mg by atomizer (1 mg per nostril); IM auto-injector per protocol. Goal is adequate breathing; repeat in 2-3 min as needed
Adsorbs (binds) some ingested poisons. Removed from many EMT protocols. Not for altered mental status, unable to swallow, acids/alkalis, or hydrocarbons

cards.front: Activated charcoal dose (only where protocol allows)
cards.back: About 1 g/kg (adult 25-50 g; child 12.5-25 g); shake well. Only where local protocol and medical direction/poison control still allow it
Doses are weight-based; use a length-based tape or known weight, never guess; use only protocol-approved pediatric doses and devices

cards.front: Medications EMTs may assist a patient with
cards.back: Patient-prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, nitroglycerin, and metered-dose inhaler (albuterol); others per local protocol and medical direction
Side effect = unintended, often predictable effect; adverse reaction = harmful unintended response
Patient verbally or in writing agrees to care (competent adult, informed)
Presumed consent for life-threatening emergency when patient unresponsive or unable to decide
Patient understands risks, benefits, and alternatives before agreeing
Parent/guardian consents; emergency treatment proceeds under implied consent if none available
Minor legally treated as an adult (e.g., married, in the military, court order; in some states pregnant or a parent); can consent. Criteria vary by state
Court- or law-enforcement-ordered treatment, e.g., for prisoners or dangerous patients
Competent adult can refuse; ensure informed refusal, document thoroughly, get signature, witness, advise, per protocol
Ending care without the patient's consent and without ensuring continued care by a provider of equal or higher level
Duty to act, breach of duty, harm/injury, causation (proximate cause)
Obligation to respond when on duty or called; may arise from policy, contract, or statute
How a reasonably prudent, similarly trained provider would act under similar circumstances
Care an EMT is legally allowed to provide, defined by state law and medical direction
Assault = threat of unwanted contact; battery = actual unlawful touching without consent
Unlawfully restraining a person without consent or legal authority
Libel = false written statement; slander = false spoken statement
Protects those who give care in good faith without compensation, outside duty; not for gross negligence
Protects the privacy of patient health information; PHI may be released for treatment, payment, operations, or as required by law
Any identifiable info about a patient's health, care, or payment
Child abuse/neglect; elder or vulnerable adult abuse; in many states gunshot/stab wounds, sexual assault, animal bites, some communicable diseases. Varies by state
Written order to withhold CPR/resuscitation; must be valid per state law and local protocol. DNR does not mean do not treat: still give comfort care
Portable medical orders for seriously ill patients detailing limits of treatment; follow per protocol
Patient's written wishes about future care if incapacitated

cards.front: Durable power of attorney for health care
cards.back: Person authorized to make medical decisions when the patient cannot
Online = real-time contact with a physician; off-line = standing orders and protocols
Ensure scene safety, treat the patient, avoid disturbing evidence, document and report observations
Decapitation, rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition, incineration (per protocol)
Record capacity assessment, risks explained, patient statements, witness, and signature
Provide care; do not delay resuscitation; follow local protocol, notify hospital of donor status
Use only reasonable force, per protocol and with law enforcement as needed; document why
Latin: 'the thing speaks for itself'; negligence apparent from the circumstances
Preparation, dispatch, en route, arrival at scene, patient contact, transport, transfer of care at hospital, post-run
Nature of call, location, patient count, name/callback number, safety concerns
Only when appropriate per local protocol and state law; drive with due regard for safety of others
Commonly taught as at least 4 seconds (some sources 3); more in bad weather, at speed, or with a heavy vehicle. Follow agency policy and state law
Type I (truck chassis), Type II (van), Type III (cutaway van chassis)
Treat all body fluids as potentially infectious; PPE includes gloves, eye protection, mask, gown
Fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirator for the provider when TB or other airborne illness is suspected; surgical mask on the patient if tolerated
Wash after every patient contact; alcohol-based rub if soap unavailable and hands not visibly soiled
Never recap needles; dispose in puncture-resistant sharps container immediately
Report immediately, wash exposed area, document, follow agency exposure control plan
Cleaning removes dirt; disinfection kills most organisms; sterilization kills all microorganisms
Feet shoulder-width apart, back straight, lift with legs, weight close to body, no twisting
Palms up, hands at least 10 inches apart, fully contact the object with all fingers
Immediate danger (fire, hazmat, explosives), cannot protect patient, or cannot access others needing care
Blanket drag, clothing drag, shoulder drag, firefighter's drag
Immediate life threat needing rapid transport: altered mental status, inadequate ABCs, shock
No immediate life threat; take time to stabilize and use proper equipment
Urgent move of a seated patient from a vehicle onto a long board with manual spinal stabilization; for unstable patients, unsafe scenes, or to reach a critical patient
Used for carrying a seated patient down stairs; not for spinal injuries
Splits and rejoins around patient; minimal movement; helpful for pelvic/spinal precautions
Rigid device for moving spinal-risk patients; not a long-term transport surface
Size-up, hazard control and vehicle stabilization, gain access, emergency care, disentanglement (remove vehicle from around patient), removal and transfer
Undeployed airbags, leaking fuel, battery/electrical, traffic, broken glass and sharp metal, hybrid/EV high voltage, unstable vehicle
Commonly 100 x 100 ft (some services accept 60 x 60 ft by day); flat, firm, clear of wires, obstacles and loose debris. Follow the flight service/local protocol
Only when signaled by the crew; from the front in the pilot's view, crouched; never near the tail rotor; on a slope approach from the downhill side
Stage away until police secure the scene; consider hidden weapons
Continuity of care, legal record, billing/administrative, education, research, quality improvement
Draw one line through the error, initial it, and add correct info; never obliterate
Clear, brief, plain language, hold mic 2-3 inches away, push key and wait 1 second, no profanity, repeat orders
Age/sex, chief complaint, history, vitals, assessment findings, treatments given, ETA
Peer support and debriefing after traumatic calls; recognize signs of stress, burnout, PTSD
Incident whose number or severity of patients strains or exceeds available resources. Some textbooks say 3 or more patients; the threshold is set by the local plan
Standardized, scalable command structure and common terminology for managing incidents
Overall responsibility for incident; sets objectives, priorities, and strategy
Public Information Officer, Safety Officer, Liaison Officer
Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Administration (NIMS also allows an optional Intelligence/Investigations function)
Multiple agencies share command with agreed-upon objectives
Number of people one supervisor can manage: NIMS optimum is 1 supervisor to 5 subordinates; textbooks commonly give a range of 3-7
Location where resources wait until assigned
Triage, treatment, transport, staging; also extrication/rescue, morgue, rehab and supply as needed (ICS calls these groups, divisions or units)
Sort patients by urgency to do the greatest good for the most; reassess continually
Direct walking wounded to a safe area; they are tagged green (minor)
Not breathing after airway opened = black; starts breathing after airway opened = red; rate over 30/min = red; under 30 = go on to check perfusion
No radial pulse or capillary refill >2 seconds = red; control severe bleeding; if pulse present/refill normal, check mental status
Cannot follow simple commands = red; can follow commands = yellow
Red = immediate; yellow = delayed; green = minor; black = deceased/expectant
Pediatric MCI triage for about ages 1-8 (if the patient looks like a child use JumpSTART; like a young adult use START). Infants are assessed with the non-ambulatory steps
Children able to walk are tagged green (minor) and sent for secondary triage; infants and children who cannot normally walk are assessed with the full algorithm
Open airway. Breathing starts = red. Still apneic: check pulse. No pulse = black. Pulse present: give 5 rescue breaths; breathing = red, still apneic = black
Rate under 15 or over 45/min, or irregular = red; rate 15-45 = go on to assess perfusion
No palpable pulse = red. AVPU: P with inappropriate response (posturing) or U = red; A, V, or P with appropriate response (localizes pain) = yellow
Apneic with no palpable pulse after airway opening, OR pulse present but still apneic after 5 rescue breaths = black (deceased/expectant)
Contaminated area; only trained hazmat personnel in proper PPE enter; also called exclusion (red) zone
Contamination reduction zone between hot and cold; decontamination corridor is here; entry needs proper PPE and training
Safe support zone (uphill/upwind): command post, staging, and EMS triage/treatment of decontaminated patients
Index of materials in order of 4-digit UN/NA ID number; gives the guide number. Highlighted entries: go to green pages
Index of materials alphabetically by name; gives ID number and guide number. Highlighted entries: go to green pages
The numbered guides: potential hazards, public safety (isolation, PPE, evacuation), and emergency response (fire, spill, first aid)
Tables of initial isolation and protective action distances for toxic-inhalation-hazard and water-reactive materials (highlighted in yellow/blue pages)
Red = flammable; orange = explosive

cards.front: Hazmat placard color: green / yellow / blue
cards.back: Green = nonflammable gas; yellow = oxidizer; blue = dangerous when wet. (Yellow over white = radioactive)
White = poison/toxic or infectious substance; white top with black bottom = corrosive; red and white stripes = flammable solid
Blue = health, red = flammability, yellow = instability (reactivity), white = special hazards (e.g., W = no water, OX); each rated 0-4, 4 = worst
Approach from uphill and upwind (upstream); stay at a safe distance; identify with binoculars; isolate and deny entry; do not enter without training/PPE
Placards, shipping papers, safety data sheets, ERG, CHEMTREC, poison control
